statement: During starvation, organisms are able to reproduce, grow, and survive for some time.

scores.rationale: The corpus provides strong and consistent support for the stylized fact. Snippet [14] explicitly lists this as a set of feeding stylized facts (F1–F3) with empirical citations for animals and bacteria. Multiple snippets confirm organisms can survive starvation for some time by utilizing stored reserves ([1], [2], [3], [13]), that growth typically continues in the early phase of starvation ([2]), and that reproduction can persist using the reproduction buffer or remaining flux ([16], [9]). Several DEB modeling papers ([5], [11], [13], [12], [17]) describe the mechanisms—reserve mobilization, lysis of structure, ceasing of growth/reproduction under prolonged deprivation—that allow temporary survival, all consistent with the fact that starvation tolerance is finite but real. No snippet contradicts the claim; the neutral ones are mechanistic/equation-focused. Overall the evidence clearly corroborates that organisms can reproduce, grow, and survive for some time during starvation.

scores.rationale: Multiple snippets corroborate that organisms survive, continue some reproduction, and adapt during starvation. Several report measurable starvation survival times (rotifers [5,6], lace bug [15], Drosophila [8,10]) and describe physiological/metabolic adaptations (insects [4], C. elegans [11,16]) and trade-offs between reproduction and starvation resistance, all consistent with the fact that organisms persist for some time without food and can allocate residual resources to reproduction (e.g., Daphnia storage/reproduction trade-offs [2,17]). No snippet contradicts the fact. However, none explicitly demonstrate continued growth, and most evidence centers on survival and reproductive trade-offs rather than the full triad (reproduce, grow, survive), so support is moderate rather than strong. Overall the direction is clearly corroborative with little conflict.
